summary: Describes NAT-PMP, a protocol that automates creating NAT port mappings and lets a client learn the external IPv4 address of a NAT gateway. Apple products have implemented it since 2005. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A computer behind a router asks the router to open a particular door to the outside and tells it the address of the front gate, so friends can connect.

questions: how to automatically create a port mapping on a nat
how does nat-pmp create a port mapping
subtitle: How a computer behind a home NAT asks the router to open a port and tells it its public IPv4 address.

tldr.problem: Hosts behind a NAT cannot receive inbound connections unless someone configures port mappings by hand, which is too onerous for most residential users.
tldr.mechanism: NAT-PMP is a small UDP protocol in which a client asks its default gateway for the external IPv4 address or for a time-limited TCP or UDP port mapping, and renews that mapping before it expires.
tldr.outcome: NAT-PMP was superseded in 2013 by the Standards Track Port Control Protocol (PCP), and implementations are encouraged to migrate.

today: RFC 6886 is an Informational document that was superseded in 2013 by the Standards Track Port Control Protocol, RFC 6887, and existing NAT-PMP implementations are encouraged to migrate to PCP.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
A NAT (here a NAPT, Network Address/Port Translator) shares one public address among many devices by keeping a table of mappings from internal address and port to external address and port. Mappings are normally created by outbound packets. An inbound packet that matches no mapping will most likely be dropped, so clients behind a NAT cannot receive inbound connections. Manually configuring mappings is, in the RFC's words, unreasonably onerous for most residential users.

NAT-PMP lets a client ask the gateway for an inbound mapping on demand. The client can then record its external IPv4 address and port in a public registry such as the global DNS so peers can reach it.

The protocol is designed for small home networks with a single subnet where the client's default gateway is also the NAT. It SHOULD only be used when the client's primary IPv4 address is in a private range from RFC 1918 (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16).
sections.eli5: Normally a router only lets in visitors that you called first. This lets a computer ask the router to leave one door open for visitors who were not called first.

sections.title: Packets and Requests
sections.content:
NAT-PMP runs over UDP. Every packet starts with an 8-bit version (0 in this document) and an 8-bit opcode. Opcodes 0 to 127 are client requests; 128 to 255 are the matching responses. Multi-byte numbers use network byte order. A gateway receiving any other version MUST return result code 1 (Unsupported Version).

A client sends requests to port 5351 of its default gateway. To learn the external address, it sends opcode 0 and the gateway answers with a result code, the Seconds Since Start of Epoch and the External IPv4 Address. To create a mapping, it sends opcode 1 (Map UDP) or 2 (Map TCP) with an Internal Port, a Suggested External Port and a Requested Port Mapping Lifetime. The RECOMMENDED lifetime is 7200 seconds (two hours).

If the client sets the Suggested External Port to zero, the gateway picks a high-numbered port. The gateway is not obliged to grant the suggested port, for example if it is reserved or already assigned. The response carries the Internal Port, the Mapped External Port and the lifetime actually granted; the gateway MAY reduce the lifetime but SHOULD NOT offer more than requested.

The source address of the request is always used as the internal address in the mapping, so one device cannot create mappings for another. A gateway MUST be able to create TCP-only and UDP-only mappings, and MUST NOT accept mapping requests on its external interface.
sections.eli5: The computer sends a short note to the router saying which door it wants and for how long. The router answers with the door number it actually gave.

sections.title: Retries, Renewal and Deletion
sections.content:
Clients wait 250 ms for a reply, then retransmit and wait 500 ms, doubling the interval each time. After the ninth attempt and a 64 second wait with no answer, a client SHOULD conclude that the gateway does not support NAT-PMP. An ICMP Port Unreachable lets it give up sooner. Because gateways are often low-cost devices, clients SHOULD NOT send concurrent requests and should queue them one at a time.

A client SHOULD begin renewing a mapping halfway to expiry, like DHCP. A renewal looks like the original request, but the client sets the Suggested External Port to the port the gateway actually assigned.

To delete a mapping, the client sends the same request with the lifetime and the suggested external port set to zero. The gateway answers with result code 0, external port 0 and lifetime 0, and MUST answer a deletion of a nonexistent mapping as if it succeeded, so a retransmission after a lost reply gets the same answer. Setting the internal port to zero as well deletes all of the client's mappings for that protocol. If a mapping lifetime simply expires, the gateway MUST delete it.
sections.eli5: If the router does not answer, the computer asks again, waiting longer each time. The open door is a loan that must be renewed halfway through, or it closes by itself.

sections.title: Result Codes and Gateway Reboots
sections.content:
Every gateway response carries a result code, and clients MUST treat undefined codes as fatal errors of that request. NAT-PMP messages have no transaction identifiers; all messages are idempotent and self-describing, so an error response repeats the requested internal port to show which request failed.

Every gateway packet also carries a Seconds Since Start of Epoch (SSSoE) counter that restarts from zero whenever the gateway loses its mapping table. The client keeps a conservative estimate, adding 7/8 of the elapsed local time to the last value it saw. If a new value is lower than the estimate by more than 2 seconds, the client concludes the gateway lost its state and MUST renew all its mappings, after waiting a random delay of 0 to 5 seconds and then sending requests one at a time.

The gateway also multicasts a gratuitous announcement of its external address to 224.0.0.1 port 5350 after boot or an address change, SHOULD send it 10 times, with the first interval 250 ms and each later interval doubling. This turns hard state in the network into soft state: the client holds the information needed to recreate it. A device not currently acting as a NAT MUST NOT respond to NAT-PMP requests or send announcements.
sections.eli5: The router keeps a running clock. If the clock suddenly jumps back to zero, every computer knows the router forgot everything and quickly asks for its doors again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only a client on the internal side of the NAT may create mappings, and only for itself. Through IP address spoofing, one client could delete or create mappings on behalf of another; where that matters, IPsec can be used. Multicast announcements could be spoofed to mount a denial of service, so NAT-PMP is unsuitable on LANs with many hosts where some may be untrustworthy.

The authors argue that a NAT is not a firewall, and that blocking should come from explicit firewall policy. Because many users expect otherwise, a gateway implementing NAT-PMP SHOULD have an administrative way to disable it.
sections.eli5: Anyone in the house could pretend to be someone else when talking to the router, so it should only be used where everyone in the house is trusted. The router should also have an off switch.

sections.title: Transition to PCP and Deployment History
sections.content:
After almost a decade of use, NAT-PMP was succeeded by the Standards Track Port Control Protocol, RFC 6887. PCP uses the same UDP ports 5350 and 5351 and a compatible packet format, with version number 2 instead of 0. It adds IPv6 support, management of outbound mappings and firewall rules, support for large-scale NATs, error lifetimes and an extension mechanism. Version 1 MUST NOT be used by PCP implementations. Servers answer by version, and clients should try PCP first and fall back to NAT-PMP on an Unsupported Version reply.

The RFC's deployment history says NAT-PMP client software first became public in August 2004, shipped to end users in April 2005 with Mac OS X 10.4 Tiger and Bonjour for Windows 1.0, and is implemented on the server side in Apple's AirPort Extreme, AirPort Express and Time Capsule base stations.
sections.eli5: A newer, more capable version called PCP has taken over, and it is built so that old and new routers and computers can still understand each other.

fields.name: OP
fields.desc: 1 for Map UDP, 2 for Map TCP.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.name: Internal Port
fields.desc: Local port on which the client is listening.

fields.name: Suggested External Port
fields.desc: Preferred external port; zero lets the gateway choose.

items.label: Unsupported Version
items.desc: The version in the request is not supported.

items.label: Not Authorized/Refused
items.desc: For example, the box supports mapping but the user has turned the feature off.

items.label: Network Failure
items.desc: For example, the NAT box has not obtained a DHCP lease.

items.label: Out of resources
items.desc: The NAT box cannot create any more mappings at this time.

messages.label: Announcement
messages.note: SSSoE restarted from zero, sent to 224.0.0.1 port 5350.

messages.label: Mapping request (renewal)
